newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China domestic cotton sold cheap, less seen planted.
newsitem.headline: China domestic cotton sold cheap, less seen planted.

text.p: China's Cotton and Jute Corp was offering cotton to domestic mills at slashed prices to liquidate stocks and farmers were seen planting less this season to ease pressure on brimming warehouses, traders said on Monday.

"The burden of getting rid of these stocks is in the hands of the provincial offices or bureaus, so I think that they've been trying to obtain, basically through private negotiations, whatever price they can," said one cotton trader in Hong Kong.
"It's very difficult to ascertain exactly how deep the discounts may be, vis-a-vis what the official price is, not because it's a state secret but because nobody really knows," he said.
The government normally charged mills about 19,000 yuan (US$2,289) per tonne, while prices paid to farmers was around 15,000 yuan (US$1,807) per tonne, one Chinese trader estimated.

The Cotton and Jute Corp, the main organisation that buys from farmers for sale to mills, was offering attractive credit facilities and deferring payments for up to 90 days so that cotton mills would turn to domestic cotton, some sources said.

"Even though domestic cotton is a couple of hundred yuan per tonne higher than imported cotton, the advantage is they can take the cotton on credit, they don't have to pay the interest on loans from banks, pay the storage," another source said.
"They buy on a hand-to-mouth basis, from the local warehouse," the cotton source said. "It gives them greater flexibility, a more liquid funds flow."
The impact on imports was still unclear, traders said.
Import inquiries continued, dealers said, noting that joint venture mills often still preferred overseas cotton to domestic cotton because of quality and price concerns.
China's January to March cotton imports jumped 9.1 percent to 230,000 tonnes, compared to the same period last year, but March imports were just 70,000 tonnes.
"These figures took place before the decision was made to unofficially get rid of the domestic stock, so we'll only know (the impact) later on," said one source.

"If I was a trader or a spinner in China, before I went ahead and concluded a transaction for domestic cotton, I would want to find out what the equivalent price for imported cotton was, so there is a lot of that going on," said one source.
China would most definitely plant less cotton this season to assist in liquidating stocks, traders predicted.
China's cotton planting season begins in isolated pockets by the middle of April, reaches its peak by mid-May and usually continues until mid-June. Harvesting takes place in December.
Clearer estimates of how much cotton China planted will emerge by the end of June, cotton experts said.
China's 1997 acreage under cotton has been officially estimated at 4.56 million hectares, down by 4.2 percent year-on-year and the lowest level in ten years.
China produced 4.2 million tonnes of cotton in 1996, down 11.7 percent from the previous year, a senior State Statistical Bureau official said earlier this month.
